Read /root/agent-briefs/growth-batch-2026-10-02.md and follow its hard rules, with these changes: create your worktree on the big disk: `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /tank/nxeon-wt-backups -b feature/complete-offsite-backups main`, with node_modules and .prisma/@prisma as REAL copies (cp -a from /opt/nxeon/node_modules; never symlinks; generate Prisma only inside your worktree with a dummy DATABASE_URL=postgresql://x:x@localhost:5432/x). Notes: /root/agent-notes/backups.md; also write the design to /root/research/backup-design.md. Heavy lock: /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/heavy.sh. NODES: you may SSH to them as root (`ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no root@<ip>`: primary 51.79.162.96 is this machine, node-2 178.63.94.114, node-3 15.235.145.177, node-4 139.99.125.21, node-5 54.39.132.159) for READ-ONLY inspection only (cat, ls, du, df, zfs list/get, zpool status, qm/pct list and config, pvesh get, vzdump config, systemctl status/list-timers/cat, journalctl reads, crontab -l, rclone listremotes/lsf/about on the existing `dropbox:` remote). NEVER change, start, stop or restart anything on any node or VM, never run a backup, vzdump, rclone upload, sync or restore, never touch Dropbox contents or the rclone config, never print secrets (mask tokens and passwords).
OWNER REQUIREMENT (2026-10-03): off-site backup is supposed to cover EVERYTHING on ALL nodes, organised cleanly: the nodes themselves (hypervisor/Proxmox config: /etc/pve, network and firewall rules (nft), systemd units, node-agent and platform files, ZFS pool/dataset layout), every VM, the Postgres databases, and anything else needed to rebuild the platform from nothing. It must also run WITHOUT hurting the performance of customers' servers. Today: scripts/backup-db.sh (daily ~03:15 pg_dump of nxeon + nxeon_staging to /tank/backup/db), scripts/backup-vms.sh (daily ~04:30 vzdump of guests plus /etc/pve host-config to /tank/backup/platform), the node-agent collects other nodes' local backups into /tank/backup/nodes (step 0 of scripts/backup-offsite.sh), scripts/backup-offsite.sh replicates to Dropbox via rclone (remote `dropbox:nxeon-backups`, env /etc/nxeon/backup-offsite.env, units nxeon-backup-offsite.{service,timer}), docs/DISASTER-RECOVERY.md describes restoring from Dropbox. FINDINGS you must verify and build on: the offsite timer was stopped and disabled on 2026-09-15 00:37 UTC and has not replicated since 2026-09-14 (VM archives on Dropbox are from 2026-09-12); the timer file lives only in /etc/systemd/system (deploy/ lacks it); no freshness alert exists; Dropbox holds ~367 GiB of 3 TiB; local /tank/backup holds ~616 GB (platform 398G, nodes 100G, dump 114G); node-5's backup directory is a 20 GB directory at ~91% used; the vms timer fires at 04:30 UTC which is lunchtime in Singapore and evening in Canada (bad window); research reports with measurements are in /root/research/perf-hypervisor.md, perf-guest-and-games.md, perf-provisioning.md (read them: node RAM and swap pressure on the primary and node-4, ZFS settings, VM counts and sizes).
DO:
1. AUDIT (read-only, all 5 nodes): what is backed up today per node and per category, how, when it last succeeded, local retention, backup storage free space, which VMs are covered or silently missing (compare qm list on every node with the archives; note template and test VMs), which important things are NOT backed up anywhere (platform .env and secrets, /opt/nxeon repo state, nginx/certs, mail server VM 8000 data consistency, the Postgres WAL/PITR, Proxmox firewall and node-agent state, cloud-init snippets, systemd units, the Dropbox/rclone config itself, Cloudflare/DNS records export). Produce a coverage matrix.
2. DESIGN the complete scheme and write it to /root/research/backup-design.md: (a) categories and what each contains; (b) a clean, self-describing off-site layout, e.g. nxeon-backups/<YYYY>/<YYYY-MM-DD>/<node>/{hypervisor,vms/<vmid>-<name>,databases,platform}/ with a manifest.json per run (what, sizes, sha256, source versions, restore hint) and a human README; retention tiers (daily/weekly/monthly) with sizes projected against the 3 TiB Dropbox quota; (c) CLIENT-SIDE ENCRYPTION before upload (rclone crypt or age) because the archives contain customer data and secrets (.env), with the key kept OFF-box by the owner and a documented key-recovery procedure; never store the key only on the machine being backed up; (d) what to back up per VM: full images for platform and infrastructure VMs, but for customer game servers consider app-level backups of the game data directories (worlds/saves/configs: small) instead of whole 20-80 GB disks full of re-downloadable game binaries, plus whole-VM images at a lower frequency; make it a per-VM policy with sane defaults per game family from lib/game-control.ts data paths; honour customers' own backup settings; (e) PERFORMANCE SAFETY so customers never notice: vzdump options and /etc/vzdump.conf (bwlimit, ionice, zstd level/threads, `performance` max-workers, snapshot mode with guest agent freeze behaviour and its stall risk on game servers), systemd resource controls (Nice, IOSchedulingClass=idle, CPUQuota, MemoryMax, CPUWeight/IOWeight slices), strictly one backup job at a time per node, per-node backup WINDOWS chosen from real quiet hours in the customer data (player/visit telemetry, region/timezone of the customers on each node; the platform records player counts and visits) instead of a fixed UTC time, a pre-flight gate that defers or pauses when the node is busy (PSI /proc/pressure cpu/io/memory thresholds, load, swap activity, and the ZFS/ARC state), a hard stop at the end of the window with resume next night, throttled off-site upload (rclone --bwlimit with a timetable, --transfers 1-2, --tpslimit for Dropbox API limits), incremental approaches where they cut load (only new/changed archives; ZFS snapshot + incremental `zfs send` for big VMs as an option; Proxmox Backup Server as an option: evaluate honestly whether PBS with dirty-bitmap incrementals on a remote box is worth it versus the current vzdump + Dropbox model, and the Dropbox suitability for many small chunk files); and a plan for the nodes that are already memory-starved (primary and node-4 swap full): do not add load there without the gating; (f) who uploads: nodes push to the primary through the existing node-agent mechanism and the primary alone holds the Dropbox credential, or something better, with the blast radius argument; (g) MONITORING: per-node, per-category freshness checks in the admin portal and the existing admin alert machinery (NodeAlert/notifyAdmins), alert when the newest OFF-SITE copy of any category is older than a threshold or a VM has no recent backup, plus a failure alert that cannot be silent (the 'timer disabled' case must alert); (h) RESTORE TESTING: an automated weekly restore test of one database dump and one VM archive (to a scratch VMID on a node with headroom, using a fresh never-reused VMID, destroyed afterwards) with the result recorded; update docs/DISASTER-RECOVERY.md with a complete rebuild-from-nothing runbook for every category including nodes; (i) rollout plan in safe stages with owner approvals, a catch-up plan for the 19-day gap that does not flood the disk or Dropbox, and rollback.
3. BUILD what is buildable in the repo with tests: new/updated scripts and systemd units in deploy/ (including the offsite timer and a freshness check unit), the manifest writer, the encryption wrapper, the gating/pre-flight helper, per-node window selection from telemetry (pure, unit-tested), the admin freshness page or panel and alerts following existing admin patterns, node-agent endpoints if needed (read-only listing/health first). Everything inert by default behind flags where it changes behaviour; nothing may be applied to any node. Typecheck and tests; docs section in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md.
Report per the brief: the coverage matrix, the design decisions and why, the expected load profile and how it was bounded, projected Dropbox usage, what you built, the exact owner rollout steps in order, what you could not verify, and owner decisions needed (including where the encryption key will live).

- Owner decisions: /root/growth/decisions-summary.json (`dec` map; `do` / `change` = approved, `skip` = do NOT build).

## Hard rules (violating any of these is a failure)
1. Never edit, build, test or restart inside /opt/nxeon. Work ONLY in your own git worktree: `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /opt/nxeon-wt-<name> -b <branch> main`. main already contains the day's fixes; branch from current main.

4. Commit with explicit paths only (`git add <paths>`), never `git add -A`. Do not push. Notes go to /root/agent-notes/<name>.md.
5. You must not touch production, any Proxmox node, any VM, any customer data, any email/SMS/Discord/social send, any payment or card action, or any paid third-party tool. Everything that sends, charges or posts must be built behind a default-OFF flag or produced as a draft for the owner. Do not deploy; the owner's session merges and promotes.
6. Schema changes must be purely additive (the production deploy only runs additive `prisma db push`).
7. Honesty: never fabricate statistics, reviews, customer counts, awards or testimonials. Claims must come from real data in the repo/DB or be omitted. The "47 seconds" tagline is intentional brand copy; never flag or change it. Never mention a third-party infrastructure provider to customers; Nxeon speaks as the owner. Customer-visible copy: no "provider".
8. Brand: use existing design tokens/components (navy + violet + cyan; brand gradient blue→violet→magenta). Match surrounding code style, naming and comment density. Update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md for operational/third-party knowledge.
9. Money path (checkout, pricing, billing, Stripe, wallet): extra care. Build behind flags, add tests, and state exactly what was and was not verified. Never run a live charge.
10. Legal flags: Hytale and FiveM are legally sensitive (owner decision: no managed FiveM sale without permission). Content for these is informational only, and you must say so in your notes.
11. No overlap: stay inside your assigned item ids. If you need a file another agent owns, make the smallest possible change and say so in your notes.
12. Verify before reporting: run typecheck and the tests related to your change, and run what you can locally (a local dev render is fine if it uses a throwaway DB; never the shared prod DB). Your final report must list: branch, commits, files touched, what you verified, what you could not verify, any owner decisions or owner actions needed, and any flags/env vars to enable.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

#!/bin/bash
# Two-slot lock so at most TWO heavy jobs (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) run at once on this box.
# This machine is the live production primary (also hosts customer VMs) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers
# can OOM or starve production. (Was 1 slot; raised to 2 on 2026-10-01 because 20 agents were queueing.)
# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
deadline=$((SECONDS + 3600))
while [ $SECONDS -lt $deadline ]; do
  for i in 1 2; do
    exec {fd}>/tmp/nxeon-heavy.$i.lock
    if flock -n $fd; then
      exec nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"
    fi
    exec {fd}>&-
  done
  sleep 2
done
echo "heavy.sh: timed out waiting for a slot" >&2; exit 75

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Off-box backup replication.
#
# Copies the DB dumps, the host-configuration archives and (optionally) the
# whole-system VM archives to an OFFSITE target, so a chassis or disk loss does
# not take the backups with it.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHY THIS NOW FAILS INSTEAD OF EXITING 0
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This script used to `exit 0` when no target was configured, with a comment
# reading "not an error: intentionally inert until configured". The consequence,
# observed on this host: nxeon-backup-offsite.service ran at 04:20 on 2026-07-24,
# -07-25 and -07-26 and recorded `Result=success` every time, having copied
# nothing anywhere. systemd showed a green unit, the OnFailure=nxeon-alert@ hook
# never fired because nothing failed, and the admin portal had no page that would
# have said otherwise. For three days the platform reported working off-site
# backups while every byte it owned lived on one pool in one chassis.
#
# An inert backup that reports OK is worse than no backup at all: no backup at
# least leaves the operator's belief accurate. So an unconfigured target is now a
# hard failure — non-zero exit, systemd unit red, admin notification via
# nxeon-alert@ — and it stays red until someone actually configures a target or
# explicitly, deliberately acknowledges the risk.

    total="${#all_runs[@]}"
    if [ "${total}" -gt "${OFFSITE_KEEP_RUNS}" ]; then
        to_prune=$((total - OFFSITE_KEEP_RUNS))
        for ((i = 0; i < to_prune; i++)); do
            old="${all_runs[$i]}"
            log "pruning old run-folder ${old} (keeping the newest ${OFFSITE_KEEP_RUNS})"
            rclone purge "${OFFSITE_RCLONE_REMOTE}/${old}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || log "WARN: failed to prune ${old} (will retry next run)"
        done
    fi
fi

VZ_ARGS=(--compress zstd --mode snapshot --prune-backups "keep-last=${KEEP_LAST}")
if [ -n "${STORAGE}" ]; then
    VZ_ARGS+=(--storage "${STORAGE}" --notes-template "${MARKER} {{guestname}} {{node}}")
    DEST_DESC="PVE storage '${STORAGE}' (shared with customer backups — marker mode)"
else
    if ! mkdir -p "${PLATFORM_DIR}"; then
        log "ERROR cannot create ${PLATFORM_DIR}"
        write_status false "${VMIDS[*]}" '"cannot create platform dir"'
        exit 1
    fi
    chmod 755 "${PLATFORM_DIR}" 2>/dev/null || true
    VZ_ARGS+=(--dumpdir "${PLATFORM_DIR}")
    DEST_DESC="${PLATFORM_DIR} (outside every PVE storage — unreachable by customer retention)"
fi

if [ "${NXEON_VM_BACKUP_DRYRUN:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    log "DRY RUN — would run: vzdump ${VMIDS[*]} ${VZ_ARGS[*]}"
    log "DRY RUN — destination: ${DEST_DESC}"
    exit "${rc}"
fi

if [ -z "${STORAGE}" ]; then
    {
        echo "# VMID -> name, refreshed $(date -Is) on $(hostname -f 2>/dev/null || hostname)"
        echo "# Matches the vzdump-qemu-<vmid>-*.vma.zst archives alongside this file."
        printf '%-6s %-24s %s\n' "VMID" "NAME" "STATUS"
        qm list 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1 {printf "%-6s %-24s %s\n", $1, $2, $3}'
    } > "${PLATFORM_DIR}/vm-names.txt" 2>/dev/null || true
fi

log "step 2/2 — vzdump ${#VMIDS[@]} guest(s) -> ${DEST_DESC}, zstd/snapshot, keep-last=${KEEP_LAST}"
if ! vzdump "${VMIDS[@]}" "${VZ_ARGS[@]}"; then
    log "ERROR vzdump reported a failure"
    rc=1
fi

if [ -n "${STORAGE}" ]; then
    if tmp="$(mktemp "${REGISTRY}.XXXXXX" 2>/dev/null)"; then
        {
            echo "# Nxeon platform archives on shared storage '${STORAGE}' — customer retention must NEVER delete these."
            echo "# Generated by scripts/backup-vms.sh at $(date -Is). Read by lib/proxmox.ts."
            [ -f "${REGISTRY}" ] && grep -E '^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+:backup/' "${REGISTRY}" 2>/dev/null
            pvesm list "${STORAGE}" --content backup 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}'
        } | grep -E '^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+:backup/|^#' | awk '!seen[$0]++' > "${tmp}"
        chmod 644 "${tmp}" && mv "${tmp}" "${REGISTRY}"
        log "protection registry rebuilt: $(grep -cE '^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+:backup/' "${REGISTRY}") volid(s)"
    else
        log "ERROR could not write ${REGISTRY} — platform archives on shared storage are UNPROTECTED"
        rc=1
    fi
fi

if [ -z "${STORAGE}" ]; then
    produced=$(find "${PLATFORM_DIR}" -maxdepth 1 -name 'vzdump-*' -newermt '-6 hours' 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    if [ "${produced}" -eq 0 ]; then
        log "ERROR no vzdump archive appeared in ${PLATFORM_DIR} in the last 6h"
        rc=1
    else
        log "${produced} archive file(s) written in the last 6h"
    fi
fi

write_status "$([ "${rc}" -eq 0 ] && echo true || echo false)" "${VMIDS[*]}" \
    "$([ "${rc}" -eq 0 ] && echo null || echo '"see journalctl -u nxeon-backup-vms"')"

log "done (exit ${rc})"
exit "${rc}"
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP_DIR="/tank/backup/db"
RETENTION_DAYS="${NXEON_DB_RETENTION_DAYS:-14}"
DATABASES=(nxeon nxeon_staging)
TS="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"

mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

log() { echo "[$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z)] $*"; }

rc=0
for db in "${DATABASES[@]}"; do
    if ! sudo -u postgres psql -tAc "SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname='${db}'" | grep -q 1; then
        log "database '${db}' not present, skipping"
        continue
    fi

    dest="${BACKUP_DIR}/${db}-${TS}.sql.gz"
    tmp="${dest}.partial"
    log "dumping '${db}' -> ${dest}"
    if sudo -u postgres pg_dump --no-owner --no-privileges "$db" | gzip -c > "$tmp"; then
        mv "$tmp" "$dest"
        if gunzip -t "$dest"; then
            log "OK ${dest} ($(du -h "$dest" | cut -f1))"
        else
            log "ERROR gunzip -t failed for ${dest}"
            rc=1
        fi
    else
        log "ERROR pg_dump failed for '${db}'"
        rm -f "$tmp"
        rc=1
    fi
done

log "pruning dumps older than ${RETENTION_DAYS} days in ${BACKUP_DIR}"
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.sql.gz' -mtime "+${RETENTION_DAYS}" -print -delete || true

log "done (exit ${rc})"
exit "$rc"

[Unit]
Description=Nxeon PostgreSQL logical backups (nxeon + nxeon_staging)
Wants=postgresql.service
After=postgresql.service
OnFailure=nxeon-alert@%n.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/nxeon/scripts/backup-db.sh
Nice=10
IOSchedulingClass=best-effort
IOSchedulingPriority=7
# See nxeon-backup-vms.service — Type=oneshot defaults to an infinite start
# timeout, so a hung pg_dump would silently stop all future DB backups.
TimeoutStartSec=2h
[Unit]
Description=Nxeon off-site backup replication
OnFailure=nxeon-alert@%n.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/nxeon/scripts/backup-offsite.sh
Nice=10
IOSchedulingClass=best-effort
IOSchedulingPriority=7
# A stalled TCP connection to the off-site target must not park this oneshot in
# "activating" forever — that would suppress every later trigger while never
# firing OnFailure=. 4h covers a first full upload of the VM archives over a slow
# link; a run that exceeds it is a genuine problem the admins should hear about.
TimeoutStartSec=4h
[Unit]
Description=Nxeon whole-system backup (/etc/pve + every guest via vzdump)
Wants=pve-cluster.service
After=pve-cluster.service pvedaemon.service
OnFailure=nxeon-alert@%n.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/nxeon/scripts/backup-vms.sh
Nice=10
IOSchedulingClass=best-effort
IOSchedulingPriority=7
# Type=oneshot defaults to TimeoutStartUSec=infinity. That is a second silent-stall
# mode on top of the never-fired timer: if vzdump wedges (network-dark storage,
# half-open QMP), the unit sits in "activating" forever, systemd refuses to start
# an already-active oneshot so every subsequent daily trigger is skipped, and
# OnFailure= never fires because nothing has failed. One hung run would mean no
# backups again, indefinitely, showing no error. 6h is ~35x the observed 04:31 run
# (3m29s CPU / ~5min wall for 6 guests) and comfortable for 16 including templates.
TimeoutStartSec=6h
[Unit]
Description=Nxeon daily whole-system backup (host config + every guest, ~04:30)
# ROOT CAUSE THIS FILE FIXES — whole-system backups had NEVER run.
#
# This timer previously read `OnCalendar=Sun *-*-* 04:30:00`. It was enabled at
# 2026-07-23 11:36:20 UTC, a THURSDAY, so its first eligible fire was Sunday
# 2026-07-26 04:30 — three days later. `Persistent=true` did not back-fill,
# because Persistent= only replays an elapse that was *missed while the timer was
# inactive*, and that is computed from
# /var/lib/systemd/timers/stamp-nxeon-backup-vms.timer, which did not exist until
# the first genuine trigger wrote it. A never-triggered timer has no missed
# elapse to replay. Nothing was misconfigured; the weekly schedule itself
# guaranteed a multi-day window in which a live host with real customer VMs held
# zero whole-VM backups, and `OnFailure=nxeon-alert@` could not report it because
# a unit that never runs never fails.
#
# Daily is the owner's stated cadence ("back up the entire system once every day,
# store the latest 3") and it also bounds this failure class: the worst case for a
# freshly installed daily timer is under 24 hours instead of a week.
#
# After enabling this timer, run the unit once by hand — `systemctl start
# nxeon-backup-vms.service` — rather than waiting for the window. /admin/backups
# flags any timer whose LastTriggerUSec is empty precisely so this is visible.

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 04:30:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=600

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
[Service]
# Owner's stated policy: "back up the entire system once every day, store the
# latest 3." This was NXEON_VM_BACKUP_KEEP=2 (and the timer was weekly), so the
# platform kept two weekly copies instead of three daily ones. The script's own
# default is 3; this drop-in is kept explicit because it is where an operator
# looks to change retention.
Environment=NXEON_VM_BACKUP_KEEP=3
# Include the OS templates (VMID >= 9000) in the daily run. They are reproducible
# via scripts/build-templates.sh, but that takes hours of cloud-image downloads and
# no provision can run without them. Set to 0 to skip.
Environment=NXEON_VM_BACKUP_INCLUDE_TEMPLATES=1
[Unit]
Description=Nxeon backup restore verification (restores newest dump into a scratch DB)
Wants=postgresql.service
After=postgresql.service
OnFailure=nxeon-alert@%n.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/nxeon/scripts/verify-restore.sh
Nice=10
# See nxeon-backup-vms.service: Type=oneshot defaults to an infinite start timeout,
# so a hung psql restore would park the unit in "activating" forever and silently
# suppress every future trigger without ever reporting a failure.
TimeoutStartSec=1h
[Unit]
Description=Nxeon daily backup restore verification (~05:30)
# SAME ROOT CAUSE AS nxeon-backup-vms.timer, AND STILL LIVE WHEN THIS WAS WRITTEN.
#
# This timer read `OnCalendar=Mon 05:30` and was enabled 2026-07-24 04:10:54 UTC,
# a FRIDAY — so its first eligible fire was Monday 2026-07-27 and
# `systemctl show nxeon-verify-restore.timer -p LastTriggerUSec` was EMPTY:
# restore verification had never once run on a schedule. The 2026-07-24 timestamp
# that makes it look like it ran is (a) the mtime of
# /var/lib/systemd/timers/stamp-nxeon-verify-restore.timer, written when the timer
# was first started, and (b) a one-off manual `systemctl start
# nxeon-verify-restore.service` by whoever installed it. Neither is a timer run.
#
# Daily, so it verifies the daily backup it is supposed to be verifying, and so a
# mid-week install cannot leave it dormant for the better part of a week.
# Scheduled after nxeon-backup-vms (04:30) and nxeon-backup-offsite (04:20) so it
# checks the freshest set.

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 05:30:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=300

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

I'm concerned that node-5's backup timer is disabled, and the last backup run missed several newer VMs entirely. Worse, since node-5's root filesystem is at 96% full and the backup directory lives on that same disk, running a backup now risks filling the disk completely.

Separately, I'm cataloging stale backup archives across other nodes: node-2 has orphaned archives from VMs that no longer exist there, and node-4 has similar orphan waste alongside its dedicated 3.6T backup pool. I'm also cross-checking VM ID coverage per node against actual backup status lines — node-2 and node-3 look mostly covered, but node-4 is missing VMs 648 and 649, which were created after the last run, plus a near-empty 9550 stub. I'm now trying to work out the per-node backup coverage more precisely, starting with node-4's 128 (cs2, 130GB) and whether it has a matching archive.

There's also the customer-backup dump directory on node-2 (167G) that I need to check separately from the platform archives, and I should look at how the node-agent collection pipeline actually pulls backups to the primary — that process seems stale since mid-September and node-5 may never have been collected at all. My next step is coverage script...

27:Short answer to "what makes everything faster": it is mostly NOT exotic tuning. Customer VMs are already `cpu: host`, virtio net and virtio-scsi, NVMe mirrors, performance governor. The measurable problems are memory pressure (N1, N4), a mis-capped ARC (N2), leftover balloon floors, and CPU contention on N1.

74:- **N1**: PSI memory is low (0 now), but swap is completely full and the kernel log shows a global OOM on 2026-09-25 12:02 that killed `kvm` of VM 8000 (nxeon-mail, anon-rss 4.8 GB). Top swapped guests: 200 (1.4 GB), 8000 (1.0 GB), 118 (1.0 GB), 105, 110, 106. Host swap activity at the time of sampling was small (si/so 4-42 KB/s), so it is mostly stale cold pages, but nothing is left in reserve. `nice` 19 `tsx` jobs from `/tank/nxeon-wt-cfg-core` (agent test runs) are the bulk of the 46 % `%nice` CPU.
75:- **N4**: 62.3 GB used, 2.0 GB free, swap full, `arc_no_grow=1`. 17 VMs, 77.8 GB configured. This is the node that held the squeezed customer VMs on 2026-10-01 (per the repo comment). Currently 14 of 17 are already pinned (good), which is exactly why it is now oversubscribed: pinned RAM cannot be reclaimed.
76:- **N2**: ARC is hard-capped at 390 MB by `/etc/modprobe.d/` (`options zfs zfs_arc_max=409993216`, not the onboarding script's 8 GB) while 13.5 GB RAM is free. KSM daemon (`ksmtuned`) is active and has merged about 4.6 GB (pages_sharing 1,219,091), and is also the only node doing so. Also oldest kernel (7.0.2-6, others 7.0.14-x) and oldest PVE (9.2.2). Root pool is shared with VM disks (`rpool/data`): fine, but both NVMes are at 54/68 % wear.
77:- **N3**: ARC full at 8 GB of 32 GB RAM (25 %), 3.2 GB available, swap 1.5 GB used. ARC 8 GB on a 32 GB node with 28.7 GB VM RAM is too large. `docs/PRIMARY-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md` mentions resizing ARC to 3 GiB on the SG nodes, but live N3 and N4 are still 8 GB.
79:- Sysctl: only `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` is set by the platform (`scripts/node-canon.sh: nxeon_sysctl_conf`). Everything else is distro default: `vm.swappiness=60`, `vm.dirty_ratio=20`, cubic, `fq_codel`, `netdev_max_backlog=1000`, `rmem_max=4194304`, `vm.min_free_kbytes=67584`.

111:### 3.1 Memory and ballooning (the one inconsistent setting)
113:Running VMs whose balloon floor is still below configured RAM (`balloon` < `memory`), i.e. pvestatd may take RAM away when the host is above about 80 % usage:
115:| Node | Running | Floor < RAM | Pinned (balloon = memory) | Reclaimable by Proxmox |
124:Examples with customer game servers affected today: N5 vms 117/139 (2 GB Minecraft, floor 1 GB), 147 Valheim, 148 Minecraft (4 GB, floor 2 GB); N3 119 terraheim (8 GB, floor 4 GB), 107/122/125/126 `web-01` (4 GB, floor 2 GB); N2 141 palworld (16 GB plan, balloon currently 15.4 GB of 16), 123/103/124/129/100.
126:The repo's policy (lib/vm-memory-policy.ts, default `pin`, `balloon = memory`) is only applied at provision/resize time (worker/index.ts: `balloon: balloonForVm(...)` in provision at line 1195 and resize at line 2233). VMs created before 2026-10-01 keep their old 50 % floor unless `scripts/pin-vm-memory.ts` was run; the live data shows it was only partly run (N4 mostly done, N1/N3/N5 mostly not). Note that "pin" is only safe if the node can physically back the RAM: with pinning done N4 would commit 77.8 GB on a 64 GB host. That is the P0-1 problem.
128:Note on weirdness: VM 600 (N4) has no `balloon` key at all, VM 601 `balloon: 0` (device off), VM 8000 `balloon 4608 of 6144`. VMs 102/104/108/113/114 (N2) have no balloon key (pinned by "balloon off"). These are fine but show hand-edits.
130:### 3.2 Disks, ZFS and clones
132:- All VM disks are **zvols with `volblocksize=16K`** (PVE 9 default) with `sparse=1` on all nodes (no refreservation); the N1 swap zvol is 4K with `sync=always` and `primarycache=metadata`, which is the OpenZFS-recommended swap-zvol setup.
135:- Clones: worker/index.ts provision() does `POST /nodes/<n>/qemu/<base>/clone` with `{full:1, storage}` (a FULL copy) for everything, and `full:0` linked clone ONLY for a golden template when `NXEON_GOLDEN_LINKED_CLONE=1` and `NXEON_GOLDEN_GAME_TEMPLATE` are set. Measured by the platform on N2 on 2026-10-01: full clone of 4.2 GB 67.7 s vs linked 2.1 s; the stock 9000 full clone 24.5 s. A 67.7 s clone of a 4 GB image onto a mirror of NVMe suggests the clone path is bottlenecked (ARC=400 MB on N2, no compression, qemu-img convert style copy): treat as a symptom of P0-3.
136:- Linked clone caveat (honest uncertainty): a linked clone shares blocks with the template's `__base__` snapshot forever; the template cannot be destroyed while clones exist, `zfs send` backups of linked clones depend on the origin, and the guest keeps reading base blocks (no ARC advantage lost; actually shared ARC blocks are an advantage). Linked clones are generally FASTER to create and equal in steady-state IO on ZFS, because ZFS clones are copy-on-write at the block level.

162:Gaps: `scripts/verify-node.sh` checks ARC cap parity but does not check compression, ballooning drift, swap, or sysctl, so N2's 400 MB cap (a deliberate or stale local choice, `modprobe.d/zfs.conf`) was not flagged as "not canonical" beyond the ARC check, which only compares persisted vs live.
173:1. Immediate, live, reversible: `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10` on N1, N2, N3, N4 (persist in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-nxeon-perf.conf`). Source: kernel docs `Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst` (swappiness); Proxmox admin guide warns about host swapping with ZFS ARC and VMs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Zfs_swap and "Memory Management" in https://pve.proxmox.com/pve-docs/pve-admin-guide.html#chapter_zfs.
174:2. Lower ARC where RAM is tight: N3 (32 GB RAM) `zfs_arc_max` 8 GB to 3-4 GB; N4 and N1 to 4 GB (the repo's own PRIMARY-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md already proposed this, but live nodes are still 8 GB). Live: `echo 4294967296 > /sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_arc_max`, persist in `/etc/modprobe.d/zfs-arc.conf` (+ `update-initramfs -u` on root-on-ZFS N2).
175:3. Re-balance: N5 has 21 GB free RAM and a 10 Gb link, N3 has about 3 GB, N2 13 GB. Target host reserve of at least 4-6 GB (plus ARC) so that sum(pinned VM RAM) <= RAM - ARC - 4 GB: N1 <= 52 GB, N4 <= 52 GB (today 66 and 77.8). Move or stop placing on N4; the scheduler's RAM guard (lib/node-ram-guard.ts) should be set to refuse N1/N4 for new RAM. Moves need a VM downtime window (non-clustered; the repo has a VM move engine).
176:4. N1 swap: see P2-2.
178:Benefit: eliminates swap-in latency (milliseconds per fault) for qemu pages and the OOM-kill class of failure that already took out the mail VM. Risk: swappiness=10 means the kernel will reclaim page cache earlier rather than swap; with the stale full swap it changes little immediately. Rollback: `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=60`. Measure: `vmstat 5` (si/so), `cat /proc/pressure/memory`, `grep -E 'SwapFree|MemAvailable' /proc/meminfo`, per-VM `VmSwap` from `/proc/<pid>/status`; journal `journalctl -k | grep -i oom`.
180:### P0-2. Remove leftover balloon floors (pin all customer VMs)
182:What: for each running customer VM with `balloon` < `memory`: `qm set <id> --balloon <memory>` (live; the repo documents this as live, no reboot, and notes that a monitor `balloon` command alone is undone by pvestatd). `scripts/pin-vm-memory.ts` already exists for this. Do it node by node AFTER P0-1 capacity is available (N1 would grow by 26 GB of commit: do not run on N1 until load is moved).
184:Benefit: honours paid RAM, ends the "1.82 GiB is not enough memory" class of game crash. Risk: host RAM demand rises by the "reclaimable" figures above (N1 +26 GB, N2 +20 GB, N3 +12 GB, N4 +6 GB, N5 +8 GB). N3 and N1 cannot absorb that today. Rollback: restore the old value. Measure: guest `free -m`, host `free -m`, `pvesh get /nodes/<n>/qemu/<id>/status/current` (`balloon`, `maxmem`).
186:Alternative honest option (owner decision): if capacity cannot be added, a smaller number of VMs per node is the only real fix; ballooning is a symptom.
188:### P0-3. N2 ARC cap
190:What: `echo 4294967296 > /sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_arc_max` (4 GB), then `echo 'options zfs zfs_arc_max=4294967296' > /etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf` and `update-initramfs -u -k all` (root on ZFS: must be in the initramfs). 13.5 GB RAM is free today; N2 has 67.6 GB committed on 64 GB with ksmtuned merging; if P0-2 is applied on N2 the free RAM disappears, so 3-4 GB is the realistic ceiling there. Also decide on KSM: `ksmtuned` is active but `run=0`; KSM saves about 4.6 GB at the cost of CPU and is known to add latency jitter and a side-channel risk across tenants (Proxmox docs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Kernel_Samepage_Merging_(KSM)). Recommend leaving it off for game/latency-sensitive tenants, or keep as the emergency valve.
192:Benefit: ARC hit ratio rises, VM reads and clones are served from RAM (OpenZFS docs: https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/Performance%20and%20Tuning/Module%20Parameters.html#zfs-arc-max). Risk: low (live and reversible; ARC shrinks on demand). Canary: it is N2 alone. Measure: `awk '/^(hits|misses|size)/' /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats` before/after over the same hours; `arc_summary`; clone time of one template.
202:### P1-2. ZFS `compression=lz4` on the NVMe data pool (N1, N3, N4, N5)
204:What: `zfs set compression=lz4 data` (N1: `data/vms` inherits from `data`). Only newly written blocks are compressed; no downtime. lz4 is the OpenZFS default recommendation for general datasets and typically is net-positive or neutral for IO, as the CPU cost is tiny and it reduces writes (https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/Performance%20and%20Tuning/Workload%20Tuning.html). It also extends the life of the worn NVMes (P1-4). Caveat: VM disk images with already-compressed game data do not shrink; zero-filled or sparse regions do. Risk: very low; uses a little CPU on N1/N4 that already have CPU contention (N1 PSI 66 %: but lz4 costs well under 1 core at these write rates). Rollback: `zfs set compression=off data` (already-written blocks stay compressed, still readable). Measure: `zfs get compressratio`, `zpool iostat -v 5`, `zpool list` capacity.
222:`zpool set autotrim=on data` (rpool on N2) or a monthly `zpool trim data` via cron/systemd (trim is IO-light but not free). Guests use `discard=on`, which frees zvol blocks, but with `autotrim=off` the NVMe controller is never told; sustained write performance is better when it knows free space. Docs: `man zpoolprops` (autotrim), https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/man/master/7/zpoolprops.7.html. On N1 `fstrim.timer` exists for the host root fs only. Risk: low-medium (TRIM load; some drives have slow TRIM); canary on N5 then N3. Measure: `zpool iostat -r`, `zpool status -t`.
224:### P2-2. N1 swap
226:N1 swap is an 8 GB zvol on the busiest VM pool, plus 2x1 GB NVMe partitions, all full. OpenZFS notes that swap on ZVOL can deadlock under heavy memory pressure (https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/issues/7734 and the Proxmox wiki https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Zfs_swap). Prefer a raw swap partition on NVMe, sized small (swap is a safety valve, not capacity). Do not remove swap without first fixing P0-1 or the next spike OOM-kills a VM. Needs a planned change; do on N1 only after load is moved.
239:- Hugepages (HugeTLB) for VMs: THP is already giving qemu 8-11 GB of transparent huge pages (AnonHugePages). Static hugepages would remove the ability to balloon/overcommit and need a reboot; not worth it.
244:- ZFS special/log/cache devices: there are no spare devices (2 NVMe + 1 HDD per node); L2ARC would cost ARC RAM, which is scarce. A SLOG is useless since `sync=standard` zvols with cache=none guests mostly do async writes.
252:1. Start a 24-48 h baseline: run `sar`/sysstat (confirmed on N1 only; `sar` is missing on N3/N4/N5) or simply log every 60 s to a file: `/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}`, `vmstat 1 2`, `/proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats` (hits/misses/size), `zpool iostat -v 1 2`, `/proc/meminfo` (MemAvailable, SwapFree), `ip -s link` on uplink + `tap*`. PSI (`avg10/avg60/avg300`) is the single best "is it slow" metric: it measures real stall time, not utilisation.
254:3. Per-change metric: P0-1 swap-in/out rate + `memory some` PSI + OOM count; P0-3 ARC hit ratio + clone time; P1-1 `zpool iostat -l` write/read wait and guest `iostat -x`; P1-2 `compressratio` + device write bytes (`smartctl` Data Units Written delta per day); P1-3 tap drops + guest softirq; P1-5 CPU PSI.
262:- **Pool fullness**: N1 `data` 68 % full with 70 % fragmentation, N4 `data` 65 % full: ZFS write performance degrades from about 80 % and with high fragmentation. N1/N4 are at the edge for 16 K random-write VM workloads. Free space or add capacity before 80 %; `refreservation=none` plus sparse zvols mean "free" is overcommitted (sum of volsizes vs pool size should be checked: N1 provisioned zvols are about 700 GB nominal on a 358 GB pool; thin provisioning risk of pool-full stalls).
269:- The N4 balloon per-VM live loop in my probe stopped early (4 of 17 shown), so live balloon values for N4 come from `qm config` only; they were consistent with 14 of 17 pinned.
273:1. `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10` on N1-N4 (and persist in a sysctl.d file).

set -uo pipefail

DEST_DIR="${NXEON_PLATFORM_BACKUP_DIR:-/tank/backup/platform}"
STATUS_DIR="${NXEON_BACKUP_STATUS_DIR:-/tank/backup/status}"
KEEP_LAST="${NXEON_CONFIG_BACKUP_KEEP:-3}"
TS="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
DEST="${DEST_DIR}/host-config-${TS}.tar.gz"

log() { echo "[$(date -Is)] $*"; }

mkdir -p "${DEST_DIR}" "${STATUS_DIR}" || { log "FAIL: cannot create ${DEST_DIR}"; exit 1; }
chmod 755 "${DEST_DIR}" "${STATUS_DIR}" 2>/dev/null || true

if [ ! -d /etc/pve ]; then
    log "FAIL: /etc/pve does not exist — is this a Proxmox host?"
    exit 1
fi

work="$(mktemp -d /tmp/nxeon-config-backup.XXXXXX)" || { log "FAIL: mktemp"; exit 1; }
trap 'rm -rf "${work}"' EXIT
snap="${work}/state"
mkdir -p "${snap}"

{
    echo "# Nxeon host state snapshot — ${TS}"
    echo "# hostname: $(hostname -f 2>/dev/null || hostname)"
} > "${snap}/README.txt"

pveversion -v            >"${snap}/pveversion.txt"      2>&1 || true
pvesm status             >"${snap}/pvesm-status.txt"    2>&1 || true
qm list                  >"${snap}/qm-list.txt"         2>&1 || true
zpool status             >"${snap}/zpool-status.txt"    2>&1 || true
zfs list -o name,used,avail,mountpoint >"${snap}/zfs-list.txt" 2>&1 || true
ip -o addr               >"${snap}/ip-addr.txt"         2>&1 || true
ip route                 >"${snap}/ip-route.txt"        2>&1 || true
iptables-save            >"${snap}/iptables-save.txt"   2>&1 || true
systemctl list-unit-files 'nxeon*' --no-legend >"${snap}/nxeon-units.txt" 2>&1 || true
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT >"${snap}/lsblk.txt" 2>&1 || true

PATHS=(
    /etc/pve                        # VM/CT definitions, storage.cfg, user.cfg, firewall, priv/
    /etc/nxeon                      # panel env: offsite target, Cloudflare, mail, TLS
    /etc/network/interfaces         # bridges the guests are attached to
    /etc/hostname
    /etc/hosts
    /etc/fstab
    /etc/resolv.conf
)
for p in /opt/nxeon/.env /etc/nginx /etc/postfix /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d /var/spool/cron/crontabs; do
    [ -e "$p" ] && PATHS+=("$p")
done
mapfile -t NXEON_UNITS < <(find /etc/systemd/system -maxdepth 2 -name 'nxeon-*' 2>/dev/null)

tmp="${DEST}.partial"
( umask 077
  tar -czf "${tmp}" \
      --warning=no-file-changed --warning=no-file-ignored \
      -C "${work}" state \
      "${PATHS[@]}" "${NXEON_UNITS[@]}" 2>"${work}/tar.err" )
rc=$?

if [ "${rc}" -ge 2 ] || [ ! -s "${tmp}" ]; then
    log "FAIL: tar exited ${rc}"
    sed -n '1,20p' "${work}/tar.err" 2>/dev/null | while read -r l; do log "  tar: ${l}"; done
    rm -f "${tmp}"
    printf '{"ok":false,"at":"%s","error":"tar exited %s"}\n' "$(date -Is)" "${rc}" \
        > "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json"
    chmod 644 "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json" 2>/dev/null || true
    exit 1
fi
[ "${rc}" -eq 1 ] && log "note: tar reported files changed during read (expected for /etc/pve)"

mv "${tmp}" "${DEST}"
chmod 600 "${DEST}"

if ! tar -tzf "${DEST}" >"${work}/list.txt" 2>&1; then
    log "FAIL: ${DEST} is not a readable gzip archive"
    printf '{"ok":false,"at":"%s","error":"archive unreadable"}\n' "$(date -Is)" \
        > "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json"
    chmod 644 "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json" 2>/dev/null || true
    exit 1
fi
confs=$(grep -cE 'etc/pve/(nodes/[^/]+/)?qemu-server/[0-9]+\.conf$' "${work}/list.txt" || true)
if [ "${confs}" -lt 1 ]; then
    log "FAIL: ${DEST} contains no /etc/pve/qemu-server/*.conf — VM definitions missing"
    printf '{"ok":false,"at":"%s","error":"no VM definitions in archive"}\n' "$(date -Is)" \
        > "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json"
    chmod 644 "${STATUS_DIR}/host-config.json" 2>/dev/null || true
    exit 1
fi

size=$(stat -c%s "${DEST}")
log "OK ${DEST} (${size} bytes, ${confs} VM definition(s))"

mapfile -t old < <(ls -1t "${DEST_DIR}"/host-config-*.tar.gz 2>/dev/null | tail -n "+$((KEEP_LAST + 1))")
for f in "${old[@]:-}"; do
    [ -n "${f}" ] || continue
    log "pruning ${f} (keep-last=${KEEP_LAST})"

I'm also thinking through client-side encryption options, comparing layering an rclone crypt remote on top of the Dropbox target against using age, and deciding whether filename encryption should stay off to preserve the self-describing folder layout.

Weighing rclone crypt against age: with symmetric crypt the password lives in rclone.conf on the box itself (obscured but not truly protected), meaning anyone who compromises the box can decrypt everything — whereas age's asymmetric approach lets the box hold only the public key while the private key stays off-box with the owner, so a compromised box can't decrypt any backups already made. I like that age can stream directly from compression into encryption and then into rclone's upload without needing temp disk space.

Dropbox's non-seekable chunked uploads make mid-transfer retries awkward for very large files, so staging the encrypted output locally on /tank before copying with hash verification is safer, and there's plenty of free space to handle even the largest file. I'm leaning toward age with X25519 keys, using two recipients — the owner's key plus an offline escrow key — with the private identity stored securely and documented for recovery; I still need to verify whether age is actually available on this system before committing to it as the primary tool.

There's a real age binary available locally for testing, so I'll let the test suite use an env var like NXEON_TEST_AGE_BIN to spawn it if present, otherwise fall back to a stub or skip the real roundtrip test — keeping the wrapper script simple and letting a node test conditionally exercise the actual binary. Now I'm moving on to thinking through the overall architecture.

Scoping out the components I need to build: a set of pure TypeScript modules under lib/backup/ covering window selection (choosing the best low-load backup window from per-node hourly activity histograms), a pre-flight gate (deciding readiness from PSI/load/swap/ARC metrics parsed from /proc and vmstat), a freshness evaluator (checking manifest/status data against thresholds, including disabled timers and VM coverage), a policy module (per-VM defaults by game family, respecting customer overrides via game-control dataRoots), and a manifest schema module — each with its own unit tests.

For the on-node manifest writer, since nodes only ship bash-run scripts without node/tsx, I'm deciding to write that piece in Python3 using only stdlib (json, hashlib) since it's reliably present on Debian/Proxmox nodes, tested by spawning python3 from node tests. I'm also working out an I/O-efficient pipeline that streams each file once through tee to compute sha256 while simultaneously encrypting with age, avoiding a second read pass over large files.

Now I'm organizing the shell scripts under scripts/backup/: a shared lib.sh for logging/gating/status, plus a preflight.sh that reads system pressure signals. Since nodes lack node/tsx, I'm consolidating gate decision logic into a single Python script (nxeon-backup-gate.py) used by all node-side bash scripts and unit-tested via node:test spawning python3 against fixture files, avoiding duplicate TS/bash implementations — while window selection logic (which needs DB access) stays as a pure TS function on the primary, producing window.json files that get distributed to nodes so each one can configure a systemd timer firing at its window start.

A frequent lightweight timer (every 15-30 min) runs a window-aware script that checks whether it's inside the backup window and whether today's run already completed, exiting immediately otherwise — this makes it resilient to window changes and able to resume across nights via a run-state file. The main orchestrator, nxeon-backup-run.sh, handles gating, locking, and sequencing categories (hypervisor config, DB if primary, platform, VMs) with a hard deadline before writing the manifest; to limit risk I'm keeping this as a new script behind a flag rather than rewriting the existing backup-vms.sh in place.

For the architecture overall, I'm separating it into a local tier (per-node vzdump with per-VM policy, throttling, windowing, and local retention for fast restores) and an off-site tier. The current off-site approach has the primary pull every node's archives over HTTPS into its own disk, which duplicates storage (growing toward ~800G) and adds CPU/IO/NIC load onto the already memory-starved primary — so I'm considering instead having each node encrypt and upload directly rather than routing through the primary.

Direct node credentials to Dropbox are risky, so I'm weighing a streaming relay instead: nodes encrypt locally with age using only a public key, then stream the encrypted bytes through the primary straight into Dropbox via rclone without ever staging to disk, keeping CPU and memory load on the primary minimal.

The chunked upload buffer adds modest RAM overhead, but a mid-stream failure means restarting the whole file, which is costly for large transfers. I'm also considering giving each node its own Dropbox app-folder token so a compromised node can only damage its own copies, though this adds setup overhead and still shares the same storage quota across the account.

I'm leaning toward a design where each node still runs its local backup and encryption, but instead of uploading directly, it streams the encrypted archive through the primary, which acts as a relay to Dropbox rather than holding a full mirror on disk — keeping the primary as the sole credential holder while limiting blast radius and avoiding a costly full restart on failure.

I realize Dropbox's content_hash is computed on the encrypted bytes by rclone itself, so to verify plaintext integrity I'll need to capture the sha256 of the unencrypted stream on the node side, maybe passed back as an HTTP trailer or separate metadata call before encryption discards that information.

Simplifying the flow: each node writes encrypted artifacts and a manifest into its own local outbox directory during its backup window, keeping a plaintext archive copy locally for fast restores while the outbox holds only encrypted files pending upload. The primary then pulls from that outbox via the agent's existing file endpoints extended with an outbox allowlist, streams directly into rclone with a bandwidth limit, and finally needs some mechanism—either a new delete endpoint or a manifest-based pruning signal—to let the node clean up outbox files once the primary confirms a successful upload.

I'm also weighing the disk overhead of duplicating the biggest archive sets in the outbox until they're uploaded, checking available space across the backup pools on each node, and considering whether to pipe vzdump output directly through compression and encryption to skip the plaintext copy entirely—though that sacrifices the fast local restore option, so I'm leaning toward keeping a short-retention plaintext copy alongside the encrypted outbox copy, accepting the extra write I/O during the backup window since throttling should keep it manageable.

Storing locally encrypted archives isn't viable since restoring would need the private key off-box. Instead, I'm thinking the better path is scoping backups down to just the game data that matters—using the primary worker's existing SSH access into guests to archive world directories rather than trying to pull full-disk backups, since guest-exec output is capped and not suited for large data volumes.

But running tar/gzip inside the guest adds CPU load competing with the game server itself, so I'd want nice/ionice plus gating backups to windows when no players are online, similar to the existing autoupdate pattern. A cleaner node-side alternative avoiding guest involvement entirely is using ZFS snapshots of the zvol for crash-consistent, incremental `zfs send` transfers—since game binaries rarely change, daily incremental deltas would stay small.

Piping these sends through age encryption into rclone would be efficient, since full sends only transmit allocated blocks (~5.79G for a 30G disk), likely smaller than vzdump's zstd-compressed archives. But restoring from zfs-send streams requires reconstructing the full chain of snapshots, which gets fragile over long retention periods, so I'd need to cap chain length by re-doing full sends weekly and ensure fsfreeze is called briefly around each snapshot for better consistency.

Local snapshot lifecycle also worries me — Proxmox isn't aware of these ZFS-native snapshots, so VM deletion or migration could collide with its own internal zfs send/snapshot naming, creating conflicts. I'll frame this zfs-send approach as an optional stage-3 evaluation rather than the default, keeping vzdump as the safe baseline while improving its throttling and scheduling cadence. Now I need to time-box what I actually build: starting with the design doc, then audit findings.

For code, I'm planning a backup gate script for PSI/load/swap/ARC-based decisions, a pure backup-window selection module with tests plus a read-only reporting script, a per-VM backup policy module, and a freshness evaluation module that integrates into the alert sweep — since NodeAlert's dimension field is just a string, I can add a "BACKUP" category without a schema migration, following the existing node-capacity alert pattern and gating it behind a feature flag. I also want to extend the admin backups page with an off-site freshness panel.

Beyond that, I'm sketching the core offsite runner script that reads the staging outbox, encrypts, and uploads with limits, plus a new node-agent read-only health endpoint exposing timer states, VM archive freshness, disk space, and PSI stats across all nodes — this feeds the primary's freshness sweep without needing SSH, though it requires redeploying node-agent on each node. I'm also laying out the systemd units needed: a window-aware backup-run timer firing every 15 minutes, the missing offsite timer, and a freshness-check timer.

I'm now working through the restore-test script's VMID allocation problem — since VM IDs must never be reused fleet-wide, I need a safe scheme like a persisted monotonic counter on the primary starting from a high reserved range, checked against cluster resources to avoid collisions across non-clustered nodes.

I'm also sketching the remaining deliverables: the dry-run-only restore test (never actually executed, just built and validated), and the disaster-recovery runbook docs. Given the overall scope is large, I'm trying to budget it down to something like 2500 lines total while deciding on the exact Dropbox backup layout format upfront — encrypted content with plaintext filenames and a README.

I'm working through the directory structure under each node/date: a plaintext LATEST.json index and manifest.json containing non-sensitive metadata like VM names, sizes, hashes, and versions (excluding customer emails), alongside the actual encrypted hypervisor and VM backup archives organized by VMID.

I'm defining the remaining tree paths for databases and platform configs (secrets, nginx, DNS exports), then reasoning about naming by backup window start date so files are immutable and never overwritten, which makes re-running the same night's backup idempotent since existing same-name/size files get skipped. I still need to work out retention rules for large VMs doing weekly full vs daily incremental backups.

Now I'm sketching retention policy across run folders—GFS-style daily/weekly/monthly tiers differing by category (DB, hypervisor, platform vs customer game VMs), executed by pruning run-folder subtrees per category through a pure retention planner function I'll write and test, then applied via rclone delete calls with dry-run as the default safety mode. I'm also planning to base size projections on actual measured archive sizes per VM rather than estimates.

I realize templates are reproducible via a build script rather than needing full backup, so I'm considering backing up just one node's template set monthly and relying on the build script for the rest, since per-node templates are mostly identical clones—now I need to gather real sizes per VMID per node to classify infra/platform/customer and estimate the savings.

For VM images, I'm estimating full-image backups under weekly retention for non-game VMs across infra nodes, summing per-node totals to about 105GB per cycle, then separately tallying game VMs that would use monthly rather than weekly full images, coming to roughly 56GB from node-2 alone before moving on to node-3.

Continuing those game VM estimates across node-3 through node-5 brings the full-cycle total to about 180GB, meaning 360GB if keeping two monthly copies, and now I'm sketching out daily incremental data-only backups for the ~40 game servers at roughly 0.5GB each, around 20GB/day before factoring retention.
